claim: Human Alzheimer's disease (AD) brains manifest hyperexcitability.
source: Human Alzheimer's disease (AD) brains and transgenic AD mouse models manifest hyperexcitability.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing this phenomenon in human AD brains.

claim: Transgenic AD mouse models manifest hyperexcitability.
source: Human Alzheimer's disease (AD) brains and transgenic AD mouse models manifest hyperexcitability.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing this phenomenon in transgenic AD mouse models.

claim: Aberrant electrical activity in AD is caused by synaptic dysfunction.
source: This aberrant electrical activity is caused by synaptic dysfunction that represents the major pathophysiological correlate of cognitive decline.
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about AD pathophysiology.

claim: Synaptic dysfunction represents the major pathophysiological correlate of cognitive decline in AD.
source: This aberrant electrical activity is caused by synaptic dysfunction that represents the major pathophysiological correlate of cognitive decline.
evidence: The claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about AD pathophysiology.

claim: AD hiPSC-derived neurons show increased excitatory bursting activity compared to isogenic controls.
source: In the AD hiPSC-derived neurons/organoids, we found increased excitatory bursting activity, which could be explained in part by a decrease in neurite length.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1.

claim: AD hiPSC-derived neurons show a decrease in neurite length compared to isogenic controls.
source: In the AD hiPSC-derived neurons/organoids, we found increased excitatory bursting activity, which could be explained in part by a decrease in neurite length.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including immunofluorescence measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: AD hiPSC-derived neurons display increased sodium current density compared to isogenic controls.
source: AD hiPSC-derived neurons also displayed increased sodium current density and increased excitatory and decreased inhibitory synaptic activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from voltage-clamp recordings shown in Figure 2.

claim: AD hiPSC-derived neurons display increased excitatory synaptic activity compared to isogenic controls.
source: AD hiPSC-derived neurons also displayed increased sodium current density and increased excitatory and decreased inhibitory synaptic activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from synaptic current recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: AD hiPSC-derived neurons display decreased inhibitory synaptic activity compared to isogenic controls.
source: AD hiPSC-derived neurons also displayed increased sodium current density and increased excitatory and decreased inhibitory synaptic activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from synaptic current recordings shown in Figure 5.

claim: Patients with Alzheimer's disease manifest an increased incidence of neuronal hyperactivity.
source: Emerging evidence suggests that patients with Alzheimer's disease (AD) manifest an increased incidence of neuronal hyperactivity, leading to non-convulsive epileptic discharges (Lam et al., 2017; Vossel et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Lam et al., 2017; Vossel et al., 2013).

claim: AD patients with neuronal hyperactivity display a faster rate of cognitive decline.
source: These patients also display a faster rate of cognitive decline consistent with the notion that the aberrant activity is associated with disease progression.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from cited literature about the relationship between hyperactivity and disease progression.

claim: Both sporadic and familial AD patients show neuronal hyperactivity.
source: Moreover, both sporadic (S) and familial (F) AD patients show neuronal hyperactivity, with onset during the initial stages of the disease (Palop and Mucke, 2009; Palop and Mucke, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Palop and Mucke, 2009; Palop and Mucke, 2016).

claim: Neuronal hyperactivity in AD has onset during the initial stages of the disease.
source: Moreover, both sporadic (S) and familial (F) AD patients show neuronal hyperactivity, with onset during the initial stages of the disease (Palop and Mucke, 2009; Palop and Mucke, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Palop and Mucke, 2009; Palop and Mucke, 2016).

claim: Mutations in APP or presenilin genes 1/2 increase amyloid-β (Aβ) peptide.
source: Mutations in amyloid precursor protein (APP) or presenilin (PSEN or PS) genes 1/2, which increase amyloid-β (Aβ) peptide, cause dominantly inherited forms of the disease (Woodruff et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior study (Woodruff et al., 2013) and established knowledge about AD genetics.

claim: Mutations in APP or presenilin genes 1/2 cause dominantly inherited forms of AD.
source: Mutations in amyloid precursor protein (APP) or presenilin (PSEN or PS) genes 1/2, which increase amyloid-β (Aβ) peptide, cause dominantly inherited forms of the disease (Woodruff et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior study (Woodruff et al., 2013) and established knowledge about AD genetics.

claim: FAD patients show increased activation in the right anterior hippocampus by functional MRI early in the disease.
source: These patients show increased activation in the right anterior hippocampus by functional MRI early in the disease (Quiroz et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior study (Quiroz et al., 2010).

claim: Humans with AD manifest non-convulsive seizure activity/spike-wave discharges on electroencephalograms.
source: Moreover, both humans with AD and AD transgenic models, including hAPP-J20 and APP/PS1 mice, manifest non-convulsive seizure activity/spike-wave discharges on electroencephalograms (Nygaard et al., 2015; Verret et al., 2012; Vossel et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Nygaard et al., 2015; Verret et al., 2012; Vossel et al., 2013).

claim: AD transgenic models including hAPP-J20 and APP/PS1 mice manifest non-convulsive seizure activity/spike-wave discharges on electroencephalograms.
source: Moreover, both humans with AD and AD transgenic models, including hAPP-J20 and APP/PS1 mice, manifest non-convulsive seizure activity/spike-wave discharges on electroencephalograms (Nygaard et al., 2015; Verret et al., 2012; Vossel et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Nygaard et al., 2015; Verret et al., 2012; Vossel et al., 2013).

claim: Recent studies have shown increased calcium transients in cerebral organotypic hiPSC-derived culture systems bearing FAD mutations.
source: For example, recent studies have shown increased calcium transients in a cerebral organotypic hiPSC-derived culture system bearing FAD mutations (Park et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior study (Park et al., 2018).

claim: There is a lack of electrophysiological characterization of disease phenotypes in neurons derived from hiPSCs carrying FAD mutations.
source: However, there remains a lack of electrophysiological characterization of disease phenotypes in neurons derived from hiPSCs carrying FAD mutations.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of the literature at the time of writing.

claim: The 2D cultures used in this study contain both excitatory cerebrocortical neurons and inhibitory interneurons.
source: It should be acknowledged that abnormal circuits related to aberrant electrical activity in AD brains might not be completely replicated in reductionist hiPSC-based preparations even though our 2D cultures contain both excitatory cerebrocortical neurons and inhibitory interneurons, and our 3D cerebral organoids show clear cortical layer formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental characterization of the cultures.

claim: The 3D cerebral organoids used in this study show clear cortical layer formation.
source: It should be acknowledged that abnormal circuits related to aberrant electrical activity in AD brains might not be completely replicated in reductionist hiPSC-based preparations even though our 2D cultures contain both excitatory cerebrocortical neurons and inhibitory interneurons, and our 3D cerebral organoids show clear cortical layer formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental characterization shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Abnormal neuronal morphology, disrupted ion channel properties, and synaptic dysfunction underlying aberrant electrical activity are retained in hiPSC-derived preparations.
source: Importantly, however, abnormal neuronal morphology, disrupted ion channel properties, and synaptic dysfunction underlying aberrant electrical activity are all retained in these hiPSC-derived preparations compared to more intact systems, and are therefore studied in some detail here.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Changes in channel properties and neurite length similar to those observed in hiPSC models may be involved in altered electrical excitability in human AD brain and transgenic AD mouse models.
source: In fact, evidence from both human AD brain and transgenic AD mouse models suggests that changes in channel properties and neurite length similar to that observed here may indeed be involved in the altered electrical excitability (Kim et al., 2007; Palop and Mucke, 2016; Šišková et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Kim et al., 2007; Palop and Mucke, 2016; Šišková et al., 2014).

claim: PS1 ΔE9 is a point mutation in the splice acceptor consensus sequence of intron eight that impairs γ-secretase-dependent functions of PS1.
source: (i) PS1 ΔE9, a point mutation in the splice acceptor consensus sequence of intron eight that impairs γ-secretase-dependent functions of PS1
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior characterization of this mutation (Paquet et al., 2016; Woodruff et al., 2013).

claim: PS1M146V is a mutation in transmembrane domain 2 of PS1 that occurs frequently in FAD patients.
source: (ii) PS1M146V, a mutation in transmembrane domain 2 of PS1 that occurs frequently in FAD patients
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior characterization of this mutation (Paquet et al., 2016; Woodruff et al., 2013).

claim: APPswe is a double missense mutation in the APP gene leading to increased Aβ production.
source: (iii) APPswe, double missense mutation in the APP gene leading to increased Aβ production (Paquet et al., 2016; Woodruff et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior characterization of this mutation (Paquet et al., 2016; Woodruff et al., 2013).

claim: AD hiPSC-derived neurons displayed the forebrain marker FOXG1 starting at 5 weeks in culture.
source: Starting at 5 weeks in culture, AD neurons displayed the forebrain marker, FOXG1, and cortical neuronal marker, CTIP2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C) (Woodruff et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: AD hiPSC-derived neurons displayed the cortical neuronal marker CTIP2 starting at 5 weeks in culture.
source: Starting at 5 weeks in culture, AD neurons displayed the forebrain marker, FOXG1, and cortical neuronal marker, CTIP2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C) (Woodruff et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: PS1 mutants (ΔE9/WT, M146V/WT) manifested an increase in the Aβ42:Aβ40 ratio.
source: The PS1 mutants (ΔE9/WT, M146V/WT) manifested an increase in the Aβ42:Aβ40 ratio, while the APPswe mutant showed an increase in the level of total Aβ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The APPswe mutant showed an increase in the level of total Aβ.
source: The PS1 mutants (ΔE9/WT, M146V/WT) manifested an increase in the Aβ42:Aβ40 ratio, while the APPswe mutant showed an increase in the level of total Aβ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Both PS1 and APPswe mutant AD neurons showed a 2–3-fold increase in the frequency of spontaneous action potentials compared to isogenic controls.
source: Both PS1 and APPswe mutant AD neurons showed a 2–3-fold increase in the frequency of spontaneous action potentials compared to cerebrocortical neurons derived from their respective gene-corrected isogenic controls (WT/WT; Figure 1A,B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: AD neurons fired multiple action potentials in response to current steps in contrast to a single or at most a few spikes elicited in WT neurons.
source: AD neurons fired multiple action potentials in response to current steps in contrast to a single or at most a few spikes elicited in WT neurons (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: There were no differences in resting membrane potential between AD and control neurons.
source: Although we did not find differences between the resting membrane potential and action potential firing threshold between AD and control neurons (Figure 1D,E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,E)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: There were no differences in action potential firing threshold between AD and control neurons.
source: Although we did not find differences between the resting membrane potential and action potential firing threshold between AD and control neurons (Figure 1D,E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,E)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Action potential height was significantly greater in AD hiPSC-derived neurons compared to WT controls.
source: action potential height was significantly greater and half-width was significantly smaller in AD hiPSC-derived neurons compared to their respective WT controls (Figure 1F,G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Action potential half-width was significantly smaller in AD hiPSC-derived neurons compared to WT controls.
source: action potential height was significantly greater and half-width was significantly smaller in AD hiPSC-derived neurons compared to their respective WT controls (Figure 1F,G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1G and Figure 1—figure supplement 2G.

claim: AD neurons with narrow spikes fired at higher frequencies with faster decay times.
source: AD neurons with narrow spikes also fired at higher frequencies with faster decay times (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 2H.

claim: AD neurons manifest smaller cell capacitance compared to WT neurons.
source: To begin to explain the underlying mechanism for the increased spontaneous and evoked firing properties of AD neurons, we found that these neurons manifest smaller cell capacitance, indicating a more compact overall electrical 'size' compared to WT (Figure 1I, Figure 1—figure supplement 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1I and Figure 1—figure supplement 2I.

claim: AD neurons showed a decrease in total area covered by neurites compared to WT neurons.
source: Consistent with this observation, we also found a decrease in total area covered by neurites in the AD neurons, as measured histologically by anti-β-tubulin III (Tuj1) and anti-microtubule associated protein 2 (MAP2) antibody labeling, while somal size was not affected (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Somal size was not affected in AD neurons compared to WT neurons.
source: Consistent with this observation, we also found a decrease in total area covered by neurites in the AD neurons, as measured histologically by anti-β-tubulin III (Tuj1) and anti-microtubule associated protein 2 (MAP2) antibody labeling, while somal size was not affected (Figure 2A–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: AD neurons showed shorter neurites compared to isogenic WT controls.
source: We found shorter neurites and decreased branching in AD neurons compared to isogenic WT controls (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by GFP-based neurite tracing data shown in Figure 2D–E.

claim: AD neurons showed decreased branching compared to isogenic WT controls.
source: We found shorter neurites and decreased branching in AD neurons compared to isogenic WT controls (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by GFP-based neurite tracing data shown in Figure 2D,F.

claim: AD neurons showed significantly greater sodium current density compared to WT neurons after 5 weeks in culture.
source: We found significantly greater sodium current density in AD neurons compared to WT neurons after 5 weeks in culture, while potassium current density remained unchanged (Figure 2G,H, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by voltage-clamp data shown in Figure 2G,H and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: Potassium current density remained unchanged in AD neurons compared to WT neurons after 5 weeks in culture.
source: We found significantly greater sodium current density in AD neurons compared to WT neurons after 5 weeks in culture, while potassium current density remained unchanged (Figure 2G,H, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by voltage-clamp data shown in Figure 2G,H and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: AD neurons showed a significantly faster decay constant for the sodium current compared to isogenic WT controls.
source: Additionally, we found a significantly faster decay constant for the sodium current in AD neurons compared to isogenic WT controls, while the rise times did not differ (Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by voltage-clamp data shown in Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 2F.

claim: The rise times of sodium current did not differ between AD and WT neurons.
source: Additionally, we found a significantly faster decay constant for the sodium current in AD neurons compared to isogenic WT controls, while the rise times did not differ (Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by voltage-clamp data shown in Figure 2I and Figure 2—figure supplement 2F.

claim: A more rapid recovery of sodium channels from inactivation in AD neurons would increase channel availability after the spike, thus reducing the refractory period and facilitating more rapid repetitive firing.
source: This finding supports the notion that a more rapid recovery of sodium channels from inactivation in AD neurons would increase channel availability after the spike, thus reducing the refractory period and facilitating more rapid repetitive firing (Carter and Bean, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the experimental data and citation to prior work (Carter and Bean, 2011).

claim: Aβ42 oligomers or APP result in an increase in surface expression of sodium channel Nav1.6 in AD models, both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Potentially underlying these effects, previous studies found that Aβ42 oligomers or APP result in an increase in surface expression of sodium channel Nav1.6 in AD models, both in vitro and in vivo (Ciccone et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Ciccone et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016).

claim: BACE1 and PS1/γ-secretase-mediated processing of Navβ2 has been reported to enhance surface expression of sodium channels in AD animal models and human patients.
source: Additionally, β-secretase 1 (BACE1) and PS1/γ-secretase-mediated processing of Navβ2 has been reported to enhance surface expression of this sodium channel, as observed in AD animal models and in human patients (Hu et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2005; Wong et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Hu et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2005; Wong et al., 2005).

claim: β-subunits have been shown to increase sodium current amplitudes and accelerate current decay kinetics.
source: Notably, β-subunits have previously been shown to increase current amplitudes and accelerate current decay kinetics (Aman et al., 2009; Lopez-Santiago et al., 2006; Zimmer and Benndorf, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Aman et al., 2009; Lopez-Santiago et al., 2006; Zimmer and Benndorf, 2007).

claim: At 2 weeks in culture, PS1 mutant AD neurons manifested greater sodium and potassium current densities compared to isogenic WT neurons.
source: Indeed, we found that at 2 weeks in culture, the PS1 mutant AD neurons (M146V/WT and ΔE9/WT) manifested greater sodium and potassium current densities, increased electrical capacitance, and increased synaptic density measured histologically compared to their gene-corrected isogenic WT counterparts (Figure 3A–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3A–E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: At 2 weeks in culture, PS1 mutant AD neurons manifested increased electrical capacitance compared to isogenic WT neurons.
source: Indeed, we found that at 2 weeks in culture, the PS1 mutant AD neurons (M146V/WT and ΔE9/WT) manifested greater sodium and potassium current densities, increased electrical capacitance, and increased synaptic density measured histologically compared to their gene-corrected isogenic WT counterparts (Figure 3A–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: At 2 weeks in culture, PS1 mutant AD neurons manifested increased synaptic density compared to isogenic WT neurons.
source: Indeed, we found that at 2 weeks in culture, the PS1 mutant AD neurons (M146V/WT and ΔE9/WT) manifested greater sodium and potassium current densities, increased electrical capacitance, and increased synaptic density measured histologically compared to their gene-corrected isogenic WT counterparts (Figure 3A–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: By 4 weeks, AD neurons displayed similar potassium current densities and synaptic density compared to isogenic WT controls.
source: By 4 weeks, however, AD neurons displayed similar potassium current densities and synaptic density compared to their isogenic WT controls; however, AD neurons now manifested a decrease in electrical capacitance (Figure 3A–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: By 4 weeks, AD neurons manifested a decrease in electrical capacitance compared to isogenic WT controls.
source: By 4 weeks, however, AD neurons displayed similar potassium current densities and synaptic density compared to their isogenic WT controls; however, AD neurons now manifested a decrease in electrical capacitance (Figure 3A–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The decrease in electrical capacitance is consistent with significant loss of neurites in the AD neurons.
source: The decrease in electrical capacitance is consistent with significant loss of neurites in the AD neurons, confirmed by histological measurement during the ensuing week (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from electrophysiological and histological data shown in Figure 2D–F and Figure 3E.

claim: AD neurons continued to demonstrate a dramatic increase in sodium current density as they matured in culture.
source: Moreover, the AD neurons continued to demonstrate a dramatic increase in sodium current density and evoked action potential frequency compared to WT as they matured in culture, consistent with the notion that these events, reflecting increased electrical excitability, represent a true difference between the PS1 mutant AD and WT neurons (Figure 3A–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3A–E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: AD neurons continued to demonstrate a dramatic increase in evoked action potential frequency compared to WT as they matured in culture.
source: Moreover, the AD neurons continued to demonstrate a dramatic increase in sodium current density and evoked action potential frequency compared to WT as they matured in culture, consistent with the notion that these events, reflecting increased electrical excitability, represent a true difference between the PS1 mutant AD and WT neurons (Figure 3A–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3A–E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D.

claim: APPswe/WT neurons did not exhibit larger sodium or potassium current densities, increased synaptic density or electrical capacitance at 2 weeks in culture compared to isogenic WT/WT neurons.
source: In further support of these conclusions, the other AD related mutation studied here, mutant APPswe/WT AD neurons, did not exhibit larger sodium or potassium current densities, increased synaptic density or electrical capacitance at 2 weeks in culture compared to isogenic WT/WT neurons (Figure 3A–E, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3A–E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: APPswe/WT neurons did not show a difference in synaptic density compared to WT neurons at the 4 and 6 week timepoints.
source: The APPswe/WT neurons also did not show a difference in synaptic density compared to WT neurons at the 4 and 6 week timepoints (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: At 4 and 6 weeks, APPswe/WT neurons showed a decrease in cell capacitance compared to isogenic WT controls.
source: However, similar to the PS1 mutant neurons, at these later timepoints of 4 and 6 weeks, the APPswe/WT neurons showed a decrease in cell capacitance while manifesting a dramatic increase in sodium current density and evoked action potential frequency compared to isogenic WT controls (Figure 3A–E), again reflecting their increased electrical excitability.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3A–E.

claim: At 4 and 6 weeks, APPswe/WT neurons manifested a dramatic increase in sodium current density compared to isogenic WT controls.
source: However, similar to the PS1 mutant neurons, at these later timepoints of 4 and 6 weeks, the APPswe/WT neurons showed a decrease in cell capacitance while manifesting a dramatic increase in sodium current density and evoked action potential frequency compared to isogenic WT controls (Figure 3A–E), again reflecting their increased electrical excitability.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3A–E.

claim: At 4 and 6 weeks, APPswe/WT neurons manifested a dramatic increase in evoked action potential frequency compared to isogenic WT controls.
source: However, similar to the PS1 mutant neurons, at these later timepoints of 4 and 6 weeks, the APPswe/WT neurons showed a decrease in cell capacitance while manifesting a dramatic increase in sodium current density and evoked action potential frequency compared to isogenic WT controls (Figure 3A–E), again reflecting their increased electrical excitability.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 3A–E.

claim: Previous studies in vivo on APP/PS1 transgenic mice have shown that at early stages of AD, neurite loss occurs without change in spine density in surviving dendritic branches compared to WT mice.
source: Notably, similar to our observations, previous studies in vivo on APP/PS1 transgenic mice have shown at early stages of AD that neurite loss occurs without change in spine density in surviving dendritic branches compared to WT mice (Šišková et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior study (Šišková et al., 2014).

claim: Neurite loss and increased excitability occur early in the disease process, prior to significant neuronal and synaptic loss in human AD brains.
source: Thus, neurite loss and increased excitability occur early in the disease process, prior to the significant neuronal and synaptic loss that occurs subsequently in human AD brains (DeKosky and Scheff, 1990; Terry et al., 1991), and appear to be faithfully reproduced in our AD hiPSC models.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (DeKosky and Scheff, 1990; Terry et al., 1991) and inference from the experimental data.

claim: AD neurons compared to isogenic WT controls showed similar synaptic density by 5 weeks in culture.
source: Concerning synaptic function, although AD neurons compared to isogenic WT controls showed similar synaptic density by 5 weeks in culture, we observed an increase in frequency and amplitude of spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs) in the AD neurons (Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: AD neurons showed an increase in frequency of spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs) compared to isogenic WT controls.
source: Concerning synaptic function, although AD neurons compared to isogenic WT controls showed similar synaptic density by 5 weeks in culture, we observed an increase in frequency and amplitude of spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs) in the AD neurons (Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4A–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–E.

claim: AD neurons showed an increase in amplitude of spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs) compared to isogenic WT controls.
source: Concerning synaptic function, although AD neurons compared to isogenic WT controls showed similar synaptic density by 5 weeks in culture, we observed an increase in frequency and amplitude of spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs) in the AD neurons (Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4A–C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–E.

claim: The increase in sEPSCs in AD neurons could result from improved synaptic efficacy associated with shorter neurites.
source: Based on prior in vivo work on AD transgenic mice with similar findings (Šišková et al., 2014), this increase in sEPSCs could result from improved synaptic efficacy associated with shorter neurites.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the experimental data and citation to prior work (Šišková et al., 2014).

claim: AD neurons showed an increase in the frequency of miniature EPSCs (mEPSCs) compared to isogenic WT controls.
source: Additionally, we found an increase in the frequency of miniature EPSCs (mEPSCs) in AD neurons compared to gene-corrected isogenic WT (Figure 4D,F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F,H).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4D,F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F,H.

claim: There was a statistically significant increase in the amplitude of mEPSCs in ΔE9/WT neurons vs. isogenic WT/WT neurons.
source: There was also a statistically significant increase in the amplitude of mEPSCs in ΔE9/WT neurons vs. isogenic WT/WT neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F,G), but only a trend in M146V/WT and APPswe/WT neurons that did not reach significance (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: There was only a trend toward increased mEPSC amplitude in M146V/WT and APPswe/WT neurons that did not reach significance.
source: There was also a statistically significant increase in the amplitude of mEPSCs in ΔE9/WT neurons vs. isogenic WT/WT neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F,G), but only a trend in M146V/WT and APPswe/WT neurons that did not reach significance (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4D,E.

claim: AD cultures showed an increase in the level of vesicular glutamate transporter (VGLUT1) compared to WT by immunocytochemistry and western blotting.
source: Along these lines, we found an increase in the level of vesicular glutamate transporter (VGLUT1) in AD cultures compared to WT by immunocytochemistry and western blotting (Figure 4G–J, Figure 4—figure supplement 1I–L).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and western blot data shown in Figure 4G–J and Figure 4—figure supplement 1I–L.

claim: Presynaptic release was affected in AD neurons.
source: Since we had found no significant differences between AD and WT neurons with regard to synaptic density at this stage of the disease process, it is therefore likely that presynaptic release was affected in AD.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the experimental data showing increased mEPSC frequency without change in synapse density.

claim: Aβ peptide enhances release probability in rodent hippocampal neurons.
source: Consistent with this explanation, prior work in rodent hippocampal neurons had shown that Aβ peptide enhances release probability (Abramov et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior study (Abramov et al., 2009).

claim: AD neurons showed a decrease in readily releasable pool (RRP) size.
source: To test this possibility more directly, we applied hypertonic sucrose solution to measure the readily releasable pool (RRP) size and found a decrease in RRP, which can be attributed to increased basal release of vesicles from AD neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: The decrease in RRP can be attributed to increased basal release of vesicles from AD neurons.
source: To test this possibility more directly, we applied hypertonic sucrose solution to measure the readily releasable pool (RRP) size and found a decrease in RRP, which can be attributed to increased basal release of vesicles from AD neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the RRP data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Among AD and WT hiPSC-derived cortical neurons, GABA-positive staining was found in 8–15% of cells.
source: With regard to inhibitory interneurons, among our AD and WT hiPSC-derived cortical neurons, we found γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-positive staining in 8–15% and parvalbumin (PV)-positive staining in 3–6% of the cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Among AD and WT hiPSC-derived cortical neurons, parvalbumin (PV)-positive staining was found in 3–6% of cells.
source: With regard to inhibitory interneurons, among our AD and WT hiPSC-derived cortical neurons, we found γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-positive staining in 8–15% and parvalbumin (PV)-positive staining in 3–6% of the cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: There were significantly fewer inhibitory GABA-positive neurons in AD cultures compared to WT cultures.
source: Notably, there were significantly fewer inhibitory GABA- and PV-positive neurons in AD cultures compared to WT cultures (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: There were significantly fewer inhibitory PV-positive neurons in AD cultures compared to WT cultures.
source: Notably, there were significantly fewer inhibitory GABA- and PV-positive neurons in AD cultures compared to WT cultures (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: AD neurons showed a significant decrease in the frequency of spontaneous inhibitory postsynaptic currents (sIPSCs) compared to WT.
source: In patch-clamp recordings, we also observed a significant decrease in the frequency of spontaneous and miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (sIPSCs, mIPSCs) in AD neurons compared to WT but no significant change in amplitude (Figure 5A–F, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: AD neurons showed a significant decrease in the frequency of miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (mIPSCs) compared to WT.
source: In patch-clamp recordings, we also observed a significant decrease in the frequency of spontaneous and miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (sIPSCs, mIPSCs) in AD neurons compared to WT but no significant change in amplitude (Figure 5A–F, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5D–F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2D–F.

claim: There was no significant change in sIPSC or mIPSC amplitude in AD neurons compared to WT.
source: In patch-clamp recordings, we also observed a significant decrease in the frequency of spontaneous and miniature inhibitory postsynaptic currents (sIPSCs, mIPSCs) in AD neurons compared to WT but no significant change in amplitude (Figure 5A–F, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5A–F and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–F.

claim: A similar decrease in inhibitory neurotransmission was previously reported in vivo in AD transgenic mice.
source: Validating these findings in hiPSC-based cultures, a similar decrease in inhibitory neurotransmission was previously reported in vivo in AD transgenic mice (Verret et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior study (Verret et al., 2012).

claim: AD cultures showed a decrease in vesicular GABA transporter (VGAT) levels compared to WT cultures.
source: Additionally, we found a decrease in vesicular GABA transporter (VGAT) levels in AD compared to WT cultures, consistent with the notion that a decrease in presynaptic release probability could cause the decrease in mIPSC frequency (Figure 5G–J, Figure 5—figure supplement 2G–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence and western blot data shown in Figure 5G–J and Figure 5—figure supplement 2G–J.

claim: The increase in excitation and decrease in inhibition in AD hiPSC-derived neuronal cultures could contribute to network imbalance between firing stability and synaptic plasticity.
source: Taken together, the increase in excitation and decrease in inhibition that we observed in AD hiPSC-derived neuronal cultures compared to WT controls could contribute to network imbalance between firing stability and synaptic plasticity that has been proposed to contribute to early AD based on data from both human brain and transgenic animal models (Styr and Slutsky, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the experimental data and citation to prior work (Styr and Slutsky, 2018).

claim: Incubation in γ-secretase inhibitor compound E reversed the increase in spontaneous action potential frequency in PS1 mutant (M146V/WT) AD neurons.
source: Along these lines, we found that incubation in the γ-secretase inhibitor compound E (1 µM) reversed the increase in spontaneous action potential frequency, sodium current density, and excitatory postsynaptic currents in PS1 mutant (M146V/WT) AD neurons (Figure 6A–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Incubation in γ-secretase inhibitor compound E reversed the increase in sodium current density in PS1 mutant (M146V/WT) AD neurons.
source: Along these lines, we found that incubation in the γ-secretase inhibitor compound E (1 µM) reversed the increase in spontaneous action potential frequency, sodium current density, and excitatory postsynaptic currents in PS1 mutant (M146V/WT) AD neurons (Figure 6A–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Incubation in γ-secretase inhibitor compound E reversed the increase in excitatory postsynaptic currents in PS1 mutant (M146V/WT) AD neurons.
source: Along these lines, we found that incubation in the γ-secretase inhibitor compound E (1 µM) reversed the increase in spontaneous action potential frequency, sodium current density, and excitatory postsynaptic currents in PS1 mutant (M146V/WT) AD neurons (Figure 6A–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6E–G.

claim: APP mutant AD neurons (APPswe/WT) exhibited a decrease in hyperexcitability following incubation with BACE inhibitor IV.
source: Similarly, APP mutant AD neurons (APPswe/WT), which bear a mutation adjacent to the BACE1 cleavage site of APP, exhibited a similar decrease in hyperexcitability following incubation with BACE inhibitor IV (1 µM) (Figure 6A–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6A–G.

claim: Isogenic control neurons (WT/WT) did not show significant changes in the presence of γ-secretase or BACE1 inhibitors.
source: Isogenic control neurons (WT/WT) did not show significant changes in the presence of γ-secretase or BACE1 inhibitors (Figure 6A–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 6A–G.

claim: Genetic mutations leading to the accumulation of Aβ oligomers directly contribute to the hyperexcitable phenotype of AD hiPSC-derived neurons.
source: These results are consistent with the notion that genetic mutations leading to the accumulation of Aβ oligomers directly contribute to the hyperexcitable phenotype of AD hiPSC-derived neurons.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the inhibitor experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: By 2 months of age, cerebral organoids matured to the stage of forming discrete cortical layers.
source: By this age, the cerebral organoids matured to the stage of forming discrete cortical layers and displayed stable electrophysiological properties in WT as well as PS1 (M146V) and APP (APPswe) mutants (Figure 7A,G,H) (Lancaster and Knoblich, 2014; Velasco et al., 2019; Yoon et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A and citations to prior studies (Lancaster and Knoblich, 2014; Velasco et al., 2019; Yoon et al., 2019).

claim: By 2 months of age, cerebral organoids displayed stable electrophysiological properties in WT as well as PS1 (M146V) and APP (APPswe) mutants.
source: By this age, the cerebral organoids matured to the stage of forming discrete cortical layers and displayed stable electrophysiological properties in WT as well as PS1 (M146V) and APP (APPswe) mutants (Figure 7A,G,H) (Lancaster and Knoblich, 2014; Velasco et al., 2019; Yoon et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by MEA data shown in Figure 7G,H and citations to prior studies (Lancaster and Knoblich, 2014; Velasco et al., 2019; Yoon et al., 2019).

claim: 2-month-old cerebral organoids showed increased Aβ immunostaining in PS1-mutant and APP-mutant organoids compared to WT.
source: Characterizing the cerebral organoids, we found increased Aβ immunostaining and a statistically significant increase in the ratio of secreted Aβ42/Aβ40 and total Aβ levels in the PS1- mutant and APP-mutant cerebral organoids, respectively, compared to WT (Figure 7B–D), as has been reported previously (Choi et al., 2014; Gonzalez et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: PS1-mutant cerebral organoids showed a statistically significant increase in the ratio of secreted Aβ42/Aβ40 compared to WT.
source: Characterizing the cerebral organoids, we found increased Aβ immunostaining and a statistically significant increase in the ratio of secreted Aβ42/Aβ40 and total Aβ levels in the PS1- mutant and APP-mutant cerebral organoids, respectively, compared to WT (Figure 7B–D), as has been reported previously (Choi et al., 2014; Gonzalez et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: APP-mutant cerebral organoids showed a statistically significant increase in total Aβ levels compared to WT.
source: Characterizing the cerebral organoids, we found increased Aβ immunostaining and a statistically significant increase in the ratio of secreted Aβ42/Aβ40 and total Aβ levels in the PS1- mutant and APP-mutant cerebral organoids, respectively, compared to WT (Figure 7B–D), as has been reported previously (Choi et al., 2014; Gonzalez et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: AD cerebral organoids showed shorter neurites/dendrites compared to WT.
source: Similar to our 2D cultures, we found shorter neurites/dendrites in AD cerebral organoids compared to WT (Figure 7E,F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Golgi staining data shown in Figure 7E,F.

claim: AD cerebral organoids showed increased VGLUT1 staining compared to WT.
source: AD cerebral organoids also show increased VGLUT1 and decreased VGAT staining (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: AD cerebral organoids showed decreased VGAT staining compared to WT.
source: AD cerebral organoids also show increased VGLUT1 and decreased VGAT staining (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: AD cerebral organoids displayed a significant increase in action potential firing rate compared to WT.
source: Notably, AD cerebral organoids plated in a multielectrode array (MEA) recording chamber displayed a significant increase in action potential firing rate compared to WT (Figure 7G,H), mimicking their 2D counterparts.
evidence: The claim is supported by MEA data shown in Figure 7G,H.

claim: hiPSC-derived neurons in 2D culture differentiated for ≥5 weeks displayed stable phenotypes that resemble several aspects of the electrophysiological abnormalities previously observed in vivo in human AD brain and transgenic mouse models.
source: Indeed, we found that hiPSC-derived neurons in 2D culture differentiated for ≥5 weeks displayed stable phenotypes that resemble several aspects of the electrophysiological abnormalities, including hyperexcitability, previously observed in vivo in human AD brain and transgenic mouse models.
evidence: The claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript and comparison to prior in vivo studies.

claim: After >2 months of maturation, cerebral organoids showed clear layer formation.
source: Moreover, after >2 months of maturation, cerebral organoids showed clear layer formation, allowing us to examine early neural network aspects of the disease in cells that bear familial AD-causing mutations.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Familial AD generally does not manifest symptoms until 40–50 years of age.
source: Since familial AD generally does not manifest symptoms until 40–50 years of age (Kwart et al., 2019), it is somewhat surprising that our hiPSC-based models display electrophysiological features of the disease phenotype.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior study (Kwart et al., 2019) and established knowledge about FAD.

claim: hiPSCs are reprogrammed to an earlier epigenetic state and hence would lack age-related changes.
source: This is especially perplexing because hiPSCs are reprogrammed to an earlier epigenetic state and hence would lack age-related changes (Mertens et al., 2018; Miller et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Mertens et al., 2018; Miller et al., 2013) and established knowledge about hiPSC reprogramming.

claim: In the intact human brain there are homeostatic mechanisms that may play a role in delaying the onset of AD.
source: However, in the intact human brain there are homeostatic mechanisms that may play a role in delaying the onset of the disease, and these 'brakes' on the system are not present in our simplified culture systems.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about differences between in vivo and in vitro systems.

claim: hiPSC-derived neurons with early onset AD mutations manifest greater Aβ secretion and deposition early on in their development in culture.
source: For example, our study and others have shown that hiPSC-derived neurons with early onset AD mutations manifest greater Aβ secretion and deposition early on in their development in culture (Kwart et al., 2019; Paquet et al., 2016; Woodruff et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from this study and citations to prior studies (Kwart et al., 2019; Paquet et al., 2016; Woodruff et al., 2013).

claim: 3D cerebral organoids derived from AD hiPSCs display accumulation of Aβ over several months and can be maintained for over a year.
source: Moreover, 3D cerebral organoids derived from these hiPSCs display accumulation of Aβ over several months and can be maintained for over a year, which is still far from the timescale of human brain aging, but comparable to many AD animal models (Choi et al., 2014; Gonzalez et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Choi et al., 2014; Gonzalez et al., 2018).

claim: Synaptic loss represents the hallmark of advanced stages of symptomatic AD.
source: In particular, we were interested in studying excitability/firing properties and synaptic dysfunction that might precede and predispose the synaptic loss that represents the hallmark of advanced stages of symptomatic AD (DeKosky and Scheff, 1990; Terry et al., 1991).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (DeKosky and Scheff, 1990; Terry et al., 1991) and established knowledge about AD pathology.

claim: Hyperexcitability and ion channel dysfunction have been implicated in the pathophysiology of AD in prior studies in a variety of animal and cell-based models.
source: Hyperexcitability and ion channel dysfunction have been implicated in the pathophysiology of AD in prior studies in a variety of animal and cell-based models (Kim et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2015; Palop and Mucke, 2016; Talantova et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Kim et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2015; Palop and Mucke, 2016; Talantova et al., 2013).

claim: Inhibitory neuron dysfunction may be essential for aberrant excitability in AD brain.
source: While inhibitory neuron dysfunction may be essential for aberrant excitability in AD brain (see, e.g., Verret et al., 2012), we also found a contribution of aberrant excitatory neuronal activity in our AD hiPSC-derived neurons, as suggested previously in AD transgenic mouse models (Šišková et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior study (Verret et al., 2012).

claim: Loss of dendrites can contribute to abnormal postsynaptic integration of currents, leading to abnormal hypersynchronous network activity.
source: As shown previously in APP/PS1 AD transgenic mice, such loss of dendrites can contribute to abnormal postsynaptic integration of currents, leading to abnormal hypersynchronous network activity (Šišková et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior study (Šišková et al., 2014).

claim: A decrease in sodium current density in AD neurons was observed in PV-positive inhibitory interneurons, rather than in excitatory neurons.
source: While previous reports had shown a decrease in sodium current density in AD neurons in cell-based and transgenic models (Kim et al., 2007; Palop and Mucke, 2016), this decrease was observed in PV-positive inhibitory interneurons, rather than in excitatory neurons as found here.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Kim et al., 2007; Palop and Mucke, 2016).

claim: Enhanced Nav1.6 sodium channel expression was recently demonstrated in APP/PS1 bigenic AD mice.
source: However, in support of our findings, enhanced Nav1.6 sodium channel expression was recently demonstrated in APP/PS1 bigenic AD mice, suggesting that Aβ may be responsible for the resulting increase in voltage-gated sodium current in excitatory neurons (Liu et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Liu et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016).

claim: The accelerated maturation of PS1 mutant neurons may occur because of decreased γ-secretase activity, leading to reduced Notch signaling.
source: Based on prior evidence, the accelerated maturation of PS1 mutant neurons may occur because of decreased γ-secretase activity, leading to reduced Notch signaling, which would otherwise inhibit differentiation of neural progenitors (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from the experimental data and citation to prior study (Li et al., 2011).

claim: APP mutant AD neurons display normal γ-secretase activity.
source: In support of this hypothesis, APP mutant AD neurons, which display normal γ-secretase activity, did not exhibit more rapid maturation compared to isogenic WT controls.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that APP mutant neurons did not show accelerated maturation, in contrast to PS1 mutant neurons.

claim: In an AD transgenic mouse model, dendritic degeneration resulted in enhanced synaptic efficacy and increased spontaneous EPSP amplitude and frequency.
source: In a similar fashion, in an AD transgenic mouse model, Stefan Remy's group has shown that dendritic degeneration resulted in enhanced synaptic efficacy and increased spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) amplitude and frequency (Šišková et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior study (Šišková et al., 2014).

claim: Aβ peptide increases release probability at excitatory synapses.
source: In accord with these findings, previous reports have shown that Aβ peptide increases release probability at excitatory synapses (Abramov et al., 2009; Fogel et al., 2014; Parodi et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Abramov et al., 2009; Fogel et al., 2014; Parodi et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2017).

claim: Increased levels of VGLUT1 have been shown in human AD brain tissue and mouse models.
source: Moreover, the increased levels of VGLUT1 found in our study are similar to those shown in human AD brain tissue and mouse models (Sokolow et al., 2012; Timmer et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Sokolow et al., 2012; Timmer et al., 2014).

claim: A decrease in VGAT levels has been observed in AD transgenic mouse models.
source: In fact, we found a decrease in VGAT levels, as observed previously in AD transgenic mouse models (Fuhrer et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior study (Fuhrer et al., 2017).

claim: A decrease in PV interneuron activity because of decreased sodium channel expression has been implicated in AD transgenic mouse models.
source: Additionally, prior reports have implicated a decrease in PV interneuron activity because of decreased sodium channel expression in AD transgenic mouse models (Palop and Mucke, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior study (Palop and Mucke, 2016).

claim: A decrease in the interneuron population has been suggested as a contributory factor to neuronal hyperactivity based on AD mouse models.
source: In agreement with our finding of decreased inhibitory neuronal numbers in AD hiPSC-derived cultures, a decrease in the interneuron population has also been suggested as a contributory factor to neuronal hyperactivity based on AD mouse models (Schmid et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior study (Schmid et al., 2016).

claim: Multiple pathological species formed from abnormal APP processing have been reported, including Aβ oligomers, AICD, and C99 (β-CTF).
source: Along these lines, multiple pathological species formed from abnormal APP processing have been reported, including, for example, Aβ oligomers, APP intracellular domain (AICD), and the β-secretase-derived fragment, C99 (β-CTF) (Ghosal et al., 2009; Kwart et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Ghosal et al., 2009; Kwart et al., 2019).

claim: Aβ dimers or oligomers may contribute to hyperexcitability in AD.
source: Several studies including our own have suggested that Aβ dimers or oligomers may contribute to hyperexcitability in AD (Talantova et al., 2013; Selkoe, 2019; Zott et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies (Talantova et al., 2013; Selkoe, 2019; Zott et al., 2019).
